Atlanta’s ‘Empress of Soul,’ Gladys Knight, transitioning into fewer live performances

Collier Heights native, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ singer prepares for a new era, scaling back live shows.
By Tim Darnell
Published: Aug. 28, 2026 at 1:59 PM EDT|Updated: Aug. 28, 2026 at 3:51 PM EDT
Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:33
Instaread

ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Atlanta native and legendary “Empress of Soul” Gladys Knight announced she is scaling back her touring schedule to focus on family and upcoming personal projects, marking a transition in a monumental career that began in the heart of Georgia.

In a social media post, the seven-time Grammy winner shared her decision to step back from rigorous touring.

“I will be easing into fewer performances while focusing on transitioning into the next stage of my career and life moving forward,” Knight wrote. “I’ll be spending more time on projects with my husband and visiting with my grandbabies and am looking forward to this new era.”

The announcement follows reports from entertainment outlets, including Billboard and TMZ, noting mixed reviews of her recent live shows.

Born on May 28, 1944, in Atlanta, Knight’s legendary musical journey began in the choir of Mount Moriah Baptist Church. Raised in the historic, trailblazing Collier Heights neighborhood — a prominent mid-century enclave for Atlanta’s Black middle class and civic leaders — her talent was recognized early.

At age 8, Knight formed The Pips (later Gladys Knight & the Pips) in Atlanta. The group, which originally featured her brother Merald “Bubba” Knight, her sister Brenda and her cousins Eleanor and William Guest, held their first rehearsals in the city.

Navigating the segregated music circuits of the Jim Crow South, the Atlanta-born group established the tight harmonies and polished choreography that would eventually propel them to international stardom under Motown and Buddah Records.

Though she achieved global fame, Knight’s most iconic work remains permanently tied to her home state. Her 1973 signature hit, “Midnight Train to Georgia,” was originally written as “Midnight Plane to Houston” before being famously rewritten with a Georgia destination. The track won a Grammy Award.

In 1997, Knight co-founded the legendary Gladys Knight & Ron Winans Chicken & Waffles restaurant. The flagship location on Peachtree Street in Downtown Atlanta served as a community hub and tourist destination for nearly two decades.

Knight’s legacy as one of Atlanta’s premier cultural ambassadors is cemented through numerous honors, including her 1989 induction into the Georgia Music Hall of Fame and a 1996 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. The city of Atlanta has previously recognized her contributions with dedicated street names and public plaques.
